1)

Copy the assignment_step and update_step functions you wrote in the previous exercise set here. (1 point)

Code 
def update_step(X, cluster_preds):
    df = pd.DataFrame(np.column_stack((X, cluster_preds)))
    centroids = df.groupby(X.shape[1]).mean()
    return centroids.to_numpy()

def assignment_step(X, centroids):
    distances = np.linalg.norm(X[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :], axis=2)
    return np.argmin(distances, axis=1)

2)

Define a function called lloyds_algorithm. It should take three inputs: (1) X, the variable matrix, (2) num_clusters, the number of clusters the algorithm finds, and (3) random_state, a random seed for reproducibility.

The function should:

  • Create a random seed with the input random_state.
  • Initialize a vector of random cluster labels. Note that each observation in X should have a label.
  • Run Lloyd’s algorithm by alternating between the M_step and the E_step until convergence, which means the labels no longer change.
  • Create a color-coded scatter plot of the clustered data (X) in each iteration.
  • Return the predicted cluster labels and centroids.

Note: If you use Jupyter, you can use clear_output(wait=True) at the top of your visualization lines to make your consecutive figures replace each other, which would visualize the convergence better. If you do not use Jupyter, you can either find another way or simply plot multiple figures. (This is not mandatory.)

(34 points)

Code 
def lloyds_algorithm(X, num_clusters, random_state):
    
    np.random.seed(random_state)
    labels = np.random.randint(0, num_clusters, size=X.shape[0])

    while True:
        centroids = update_step(X, labels)

        new_labels = assignment_step(X, centroids)

        plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=new_labels, cmap='viridis')
        plt.scatter(centroids[:, 0], centroids[:, 1], c='red', marker='X', s=200)
        plt.xlabel('x1')
        plt.ylabel('x2')
        plt.grid()
        plt.show()

        if np.array_equal(labels, new_labels):
            break

        labels = new_labels

    centroids = update_step(X, new_labels)

    return new_labels, centroids

3)

Run the lloyds_algorithm function with the two toy datasets and their proper number of clusters. You should see the correct clusters in one dataset and incorrect clusters in the other.

Find a random_state that works (for the dataset that should return the correct clusters). Note that not every random_state will work, because random initialization of the assigned cluster labels is not the most robust way to start Lloyd’s algorithm for a K-Means model. This is fine for the purposes of this exercise set; as discussed in lecture, scikit-learn has different ways to initialize the model.

Lastly, explain why the algorithm (and the K-Means model it trains) does not work well with the dataset that ended up having incorrect clusters. Make sure you include the relevant assumption of a K-Means model in your explanation.

(5 points)

Code 
labels_blob, centroids_blob = lloyds_algorithm(X_blob, 4, 2)

labels_circ, centroids_circ = lloyds_algorithm(X_circ, 2, 2)

Lloyd’s algorithm works well for the blobs dataset, but it can not get the cirle one. K-Means assumes clusters are sort of “spherical” and centered around their means. With the blobs, this works because they follow this asumption, but the circles has one cluster surrounding the other one so it does not separate them correctly. K-Means assigns points based on their distance to the centroids, so it can’t properly separate the inner and outer circles.

a)

Create a DB-SCAN model to cluster the dataset for which the K-Means model did not work. Find an eps input that performs well and leave everything else as default. Visualize the clustered dataset with a color-coded scatter plot to see how DB-SCAN performs.

Besides the correct clusters on the figure, what else do you see that was not produced with the K-Means model and the EM algorithm?

(15 points)

Code 
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.14)
labels = dbscan.fit_predict(X_circ)

plt.scatter(X_circ[:, 0], X_circ[:, 1], c=labels)
plt.show()

Besides the 2 clusters correctly identified, the DB-SCAN model also identifies noise (which are the purple points). The points don’t belong to either cluster, unlike K-Means and EM which assign every point to a cluster.

b)

Repeat Part a twice: Once with eps=0.1 and a second time with eps=0.15. (Both repetitions should be maintained in the code and the output.) What happens to the clusters with such small changes? What does this say about the DB-SCAN model? (15 points)

Code 
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.1)
labels = dbscan.fit_predict(X_circ)

plt.scatter(X_circ[:, 0], X_circ[:, 1], c=labels)
plt.show()

dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.15)
labels = dbscan.fit_predict(X_circ)

plt.scatter(X_circ[:, 0], X_circ[:, 1], c=labels)
plt.show()

When we decrease the eps to .1, the DBSCAN splits the outer circle into a lot of multiple clusters and identifies a large amount of points as noise. However, when eps is 0.15, it makes both circles into one single cluster with only 3 noise points. This indicates that DBSCAN is very sensitive to the choice of eps, because a small change can complitely change the results.

a)

Cluster the data using a K-Means model from the scikit-learn library and the proper number of clusters. Use every random_state from 1 to 5. For each random_state, plot (1) the dataset, color-coded with predicted cluster labels, and (2) the centroids. (You should produce 5 figures in total.)

What do you observe about the clusters in the figures? What does that tell you about K-Means and outliers?

(15 points)

Code 
for i in range(1, 6):
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=i)
    labels = model.fit_predict(X_out)

    plt.scatter(X_out[:, 0], X_out[:, 1], c=labels)
    plt.scatter(model.cluster_centers_[:, 0], model.cluster_centers_[:, 1], c='red', marker='x', s=100)
    plt.title(f'random_state = {i}')
    plt.show()

The results change a little bit based on the random state. But even though there are three clear clusters, some centroids get pulled away from them because of the outliers. This shows that K-Means very is sensitive to outliers because it uses the mean to calculate the centroids, and points that are far away affect the averages.

b)

Repeat Part a with a K-Medoids model. How are the 5 figures you produced in this part different than the ones produced in Part a? Explain how the K-Medoids model creates this difference by comparing the algorithms that train K-Means and K-Medoids models.

Note: You will need to install the scikit-learn-extra library for this question.

(15 points)

Code 
for i in range(1, 6):
    model = KMedoids(n_clusters=3, random_state=i)
    labels = model.fit_predict(X_out)

    plt.scatter(X_out[:, 0], X_out[:, 1], c=labels)
    plt.scatter(model.cluster_centers_[:, 0], model.cluster_centers_[:, 1],
                c='red', marker='x', s=100)
    plt.title(f'random_state = {i}')
    plt.show()

K-Medoids results are more consistent across the five random states, and the centers stay closer to the three main clusters compared to K-Means. Because K-Means updates the centroids by taking the mean of the points in each cluster, outliers can pull the centroids away. K-Medoids uses actual data points as centers and minimizes the total distance between points and their medoids, making it less sensitive to outliers.
